nodes.label: ADR-000: Modular Monolith
nodes.consequences: Fast early delivery, but scaling and team autonomy became bottlenecks as the platform grew.
nodes.context: The initial MVP needed to ship quickly with a small team.
nodes.decision: Build the platform as a single modular monolith deployed as one unit.

nodes.label: ADR-001: Event-Driven Core
nodes.alternatives: Synchronous gRPC mesh; shared database integration.
nodes.consequences: Looser coupling and independent scaling, at the cost of eventual consistency and the need for idempotent consumers.
nodes.context: Synchronous service-to-service calls were creating tight coupling and cascading failures between payments, accounts and fraud.
nodes.decision: Introduce an Apache Kafka event bus and move all cross-domain communication to asynchronous domain events.

nodes.label: ADR-002: Immutable Ledger on PostgreSQL
nodes.consequences: Strong auditability and point-in-time reconstruction; table growth requires partitioning and archival.
nodes.context: Financial transactions must be auditable and tamper-evident for regulators.
nodes.decision: Store transactions in an append-only PostgreSQL ledger with Patroni replication; never update or delete rows.

nodes.label: ADR-003: Stateless JWT Auth
nodes.alternatives: Server-side sessions in Redis; opaque tokens with introspection.
nodes.consequences: Stateless, horizontally scalable auth; token revocation needs a short TTL plus a denylist.
nodes.context: Session affinity made horizontal scaling of the API tier difficult.
nodes.decision: Use short-lived signed JWT access tokens issued by Keycloak; validate at the gateway with no server-side session store.

nodes.when: the first asks for the second's order by id, and lists and searches orders

nodes.label: Apache Kafka carries the messages
nodes.alternatives:
1. RabbitMQ: routing and per-message dead-lettering built in, but no replay.
2. Amazon SQS with SNS: nothing to run, but no replay and fan-out through SNS.
3. Apache Pulsar or Redpanda: Kafka-like logs with other trade-offs (tiered storage, no JVM).
nodes.consequences:
• Any number of consumers can read a topic, each at its own pace, and replay it.
• Order is per partition only; the partition count bounds parallelism and is hard to change later.
• Retries and dead letters are the consumer's code, not the broker's.
• A cluster is heavy to run yourself; managed Kafka costs per partition and throughput.
nodes.context: Parts of the system, or other systems, talk through this queue instead of calling each other. The forces: brokers and networks redeliver, so a message may arrive twice, and avoiding that loses messages instead (exactly once does not exist end to end); a change committed to the database and its message sent to the broker are two writes, and a crash between them keeps one without the other; parallel consumers reorder messages unless order is asked for, and global order does not scale; a message that always fails either blocks the ones behind it or vanishes; producers and consumers are released apart, so a message schema changes while old messages are still waiting; and a backlog grows silently until someone notices that nothing has happened for an hour.
nodes.decision: Messages go through Apache Kafka (managed: Confluent Cloud, Amazon MSK or Aiven; on Kubernetes: Strimzi). Topics are replicated 3 times with min.insync.replicas = 2; producers use acks = all and enable.idempotence = true; retention is at least 7 days so a consumer can replay. Consumers handle messages in order per key: the message key (the order id, the account id) is the partition key, so the messages of one key stay in order on one partition; a consumer group's parallelism is its partition count. Kafka has no dead-letter queue of its own: the consumer framework (Spring Kafka DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, Kafka Connect errors.deadletterqueue) publishes failed messages to a <topic>.dlq topic. Consumer lag is exported to Prometheus and alerted at 5 minutes. Choose Kafka over a queue broker when several consumers read the same stream, replay is needed, or volume is beyond tens of thousands a second.

nodes.label: At-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers
nodes.alternatives:
1. At most once: simpler consumers, but messages are lost.
2. A distributed transaction (XA) across the database and the broker: rarely supported by modern brokers, slow, and couples their availability.
3. Kafka transactions (exactly-once within Kafka): only for read-process-write that stays inside Kafka; the database still needs the outbox.
nodes.consequences:
• No message is lost, and no change is published without its message or the other way round.
• Every consumer keeps a table of handled ids, written in the same transaction as its effect.
• The outbox relay is a moving part to run and watch; messages leave a little after the commit.
• Dead letters need an owner, a tool to replay them and a deadline.
nodes.context: Parts of the system, or other systems, talk through this queue instead of calling each other. The forces: brokers and networks redeliver, so a message may arrive twice, and avoiding that loses messages instead (exactly once does not exist end to end); a change committed to the database and its message sent to the broker are two writes, and a crash between them keeps one without the other; parallel consumers reorder messages unless order is asked for, and global order does not scale; a message that always fails either blocks the ones behind it or vanishes; producers and consumers are released apart, so a message schema changes while old messages are still waiting; and a backlog grows silently until someone notices that nothing has happened for an hour.
nodes.decision: Messages are delivered at least once. Producers write each message to an outbox table in the transaction of the change it reports, and a relay publishes it (Debezium reading the outbox, or a polling relay of the framework: Spring Modulith, MassTransit, NServiceBus outbox). Every message carries CloudEvents attributes; consumers record each id in the transaction of its effect and keep the ids for 7 days. A message that fails 5 times, with backoff between attempts, goes to a dead-letter queue and its owner is alerted, to replay or discard it within 24 hours. Consumers handle messages in order per key.

nodes.label: Auditable case decisions
nodes.action: record every operator decision on a fraud case, with reason and timestamp, in an append-only audit trail
nodes.rationale: Regulators ask why a payment was released; the answer has to be reconstructable years later.

nodes.label: Availability SLO measured
nodes.description:
An SLO spec generates the Prometheus recording rules for the availability over 30 days and the multiwindow burn-rate alerts. The SLI is the share of requests answered without a 5xx at the edge. The error budget remaining is what the budget policy reads.

Tool: Sloth (Prometheus SLO generator); Pyrra takes the same objective

```yaml
# sloth generate -i availability.yaml -o availability.rules.yaml
version: "prometheus/v1"
service: "order-api"
labels:
  owner: "orders-team"
slos:
  - name: "availability"
    objective: 99.95
    description: "Share of valid requests answered without a server error, over 30 days."
    sli:
      events:
        error_query: sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order-api",http_response_status_code=~"5.."}[{{.window}}]))
        total_query: sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="order-api"}[{{.window}}]))
    alerting:
      name: OrderApiAvailability
      page_alert:
        labels: { severity: page }
      ticket_alert:
        labels: { severity: ticket }
```
nodes.threshold: Availability at least 99.95 % over every rolling 30 days; a page when the budget burns 14.4 times faster than allowed over 1 hour

nodes.label: Availability target met
nodes.action: answer at least 99.95 % of valid requests in every 30-day window without a server error, measured where callers reach it (load balancer or API gateway), with requests refused for the caller's own fault (4xx) left out
nodes.rationale: A target measured as users see it, over a rolling window, is what the error budget and every other decision here rest on (Google SRE book, chapter 4).

nodes.label: Available as promised
nodes.description: People and other systems reach this element and depend on it answering. They need to know how much downtime to expect, and the team needs a number that decides when reliability work comes before features. The target has to be paid for with the redundancy it implies, hold up when a zone or a dependency fails, and survive the team's own releases and maintenance.

nodes.label: Back within the limit
nodes.action: restore service from its copies within 30 minutes, losing no more than 0 minutes of committed writes
nodes.rationale: RTO and RPO are the recovery objectives the business sets for downtime and data loss (AWS REL13-BP01); replication alone does not undo a mistaken delete, which needs a copy from before it.
nodes.trigger: the store is lost, or a mistake or an attack destroys or corrupts its data

nodes.label: Backlog alerted
nodes.action: alert the owner of that consumer
nodes.rationale: A stopped or slow consumer looks like silence; the age of the oldest message is the one number that shows it (AWS ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage, consumer lag in Kafka).
nodes.unwanted_condition: the oldest message waiting for a consumer is older than 5 minutes

nodes.label: Breaches reported in time
nodes.action: notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to people, tell the people affected without undue delay when the risk is high, and record every breach in the breach register
nodes.rationale: GDPR Art. 33(1) sets 72 hours for the notification, Art. 34 the duty to tell the people affected, Art. 33(5) the register of all breaches.
nodes.trigger: a breach of personal data is detected

nodes.label: Break-glass use alerts
nodes.action: alert the security owner within 5 minutes, record every action taken with it, and rotate its credential within 24 hours after use
nodes.rationale: An emergency path that bypasses approval must be loud and short-lived, or it becomes the normal path (NIST SP 800-53 AC-2(2), emergency accounts).
nodes.trigger: the sealed break-glass account is used

nodes.label: Break-glass used

nodes.when: someone signs in with it

nodes.label: Call without credential

nodes.then: each call is refused with 401 and the operation leaves no trace
nodes.when: it is called without a credential, with an expired one and with a revoked one

nodes.label: Callers are who they claim
nodes.description: People and other systems reach this element from outside. Whatever it does on their behalf rests on knowing who they are: a stolen or guessed credential, a session that outlives its user, a token that cannot be taken back, or a call from a system nobody vouched for each turns into data read or changed by the wrong party. Sign-in also has to stay usable, and the evidence of who did what has to hold up after an incident.

nodes.label: Calling systems authenticate
nodes.action: require it to authenticate with OAuth 2.0 client credentials, with credentials of its own that expire or are rotated within 90 days, and let each caller run only the operations listed for it
nodes.rationale: A call from inside the network is not a call from a known system; each caller gets its own identity and its own list (RFC 9700 2.3).
nodes.trigger: another system calls the element

nodes.label: Card Networks
nodes.description: Visa / Mastercard authorisation

nodes.label: Certificates renewed automatically
nodes.action: renew it automatically and install it without downtime, and alert the owner if it still has fewer than 14 days left
nodes.rationale: Automated renewal removes the most common cause of certificate outages; the alert covers the renewal that fails (OWASP TLS Cheat Sheet, certificates).
nodes.trigger: a certificate has 30 days of validity left

nodes.label: Checked on each record
nodes.action: check the caller's permission on that very record, not only on its type, and filter lists by the same rule so that 0 records the detail would refuse appear in a list, a search or an export
nodes.rationale: Broken object level authorization is the first risk of the OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 (API1); lists filtered differently from the detail leak the same data.
nodes.trigger: a request names a record by its id, or lists records

nodes.label: Conflict retried
nodes.given: two transfers from the same account running at once
nodes.then: it is retried and succeeds, and the balance is never negative
nodes.when: one is aborted with SQLSTATE 40001

nodes.label: Conflicting role refused
nodes.given: an account holding the role that creates payees
nodes.then: the grant is refused and the attempt is recorded
nodes.when: an administrator grants it the role that approves payments

nodes.label: Conflicting roles kept apart
nodes.action: refuse the grant and record the attempt, unless a documented exception approved by a second person exists
nodes.rationale: Static separation of duty is part of the NIST RBAC standard (ANSI INCITS 359); one account holding both halves of a control defeats it.
nodes.unwanted_condition: a grant would give an account two roles on the separation-of-duties list, such as creating a payee and approving a payment

nodes.label: Copies locked away
nodes.action: keep the copies in a separate account and region, under a compliance-mode lock that prevents deleting or changing them for 35 days, encrypted with a key held in that account
nodes.rationale: Ransomware and stolen administrator credentials reach every copy that the same identity can delete; a write-once lock in another account is the off-site copy of the 3-2-1 rule (CISA #StopRansomware Guide; AWS REL09-BP02).

nodes.label: Copies locked in another account
nodes.description:
In CI the Terraform plan (terraform show -json) is checked: a vault lock must exist in compliance mode with the retention, and every backup rule must copy to the vault in the other account.

Tool: Open Policy Agent (conftest) on the Terraform plan

```rego
package main
import rego.v1

locks := [r | some r in input.resource_changes; r.type == "aws_backup_vault_lock_configuration"]

deny contains "no backup vault is locked (AWS Backup Vault Lock)" if count(locks) == 0

deny contains msg if {
  some l in locks
  l.change.after.min_retention_days < 35
  msg := sprintf("%s locks copies for fewer than 35 days", [l.address])
}

deny contains msg if {
  some l in locks
  not l.change.after.changeable_for_days   # without it the lock is governance mode, which an administrator can lift
  msg := sprintf("%s is not in compliance mode", [l.address])
}

deny contains msg if {
  some r in input.resource_changes
  r.type == "aws_backup_plan"
  some rule in r.change.after.rule
  count(rule.copy_action) == 0
  msg := sprintf("%s rule %s copies nothing to the locked vault", [r.address, rule.rule_name])
}
```
nodes.threshold: Every backup plan copies to a vault under a compliance-mode lock of at least 35 days; 0 plans without a copy

nodes.label: Copies out of reach
nodes.given: the store's account fully taken over
nodes.then: every attempt is refused until the copies expire after 35 days
nodes.when: the attacker tries to delete or overwrite the copies

nodes.label: Corporate treasurer feedback
nodes.description:
Notes from the quarterly call with the treasurer of one of our larger corporate clients:

- Payroll goes in as one bulk file of about 4,000 lines. Last month one bad IBAN stopped the file halfway and half the staff were paid a day late. They want to hear about all problems before anything is sent.
- Their auditors require a second signatory on every batch; today they enforce it by e-mail.
- They would like to see afterwards who approved what.
nodes.source: Relationship manager — quarterly call with a corporate client

nodes.label: Data survives a disaster
nodes.description: Stores get lost: a broken disk, a deleted table, a bad migration, ransomware, a region down. How much data may be lost, how fast the system is back, whether the copies survive the same attack, and whether they actually restore are decisions that are usually tested only on the day they are needed.

nodes.label: Data unreadable to others
nodes.description: Data reaches the element from people and other systems and is kept in its databases, queues, files and backups. Nobody between the caller and the element, nobody on the network inside, and nobody who gets a disk, a snapshot or a backup may read or change it; the people who can decrypt it are known and few; and the certificates and keys that protect it neither expire unnoticed nor stay in use for years.

nodes.label: Degrades without dependencies
nodes.action: go on serving every operation that does not need it, and answer those that do within 1 second with a degraded result (cached data, work queued for later) or a clear "try later"
nodes.rationale: A soft dependency does not count against the target; turning hard dependencies soft is how an element beats the availability of what it calls (AWS Well-Architected REL 5).

nodes.label: Denied by default

nodes.rationale: Anything the interface hides can still be called, and an operation added without a rule must fail closed, not open (ASVS V4.1.1, V4.1.5).

nodes.label: Deployed in EU regions
nodes.description:
In CI the Terraform plan (terraform show -json) is checked by a policy that fails on any provider or backup copy destination outside the allowed EU regions; the same run checks processors.yaml, the processor register.

Tool: Open Policy Agent (conftest)

```rego
package main
import rego.v1

eu_regions := {"eu-central-1", "eu-central-2", "eu-west-1", "eu-west-3", "eu-north-1", "eu-south-1", "eu-south-2"}

deny contains msg if {
  some name, p in input.configuration.provider_config
  p.name == "aws"
  region := p.expressions.region.constant_value
  not region in eu_regions
  msg := sprintf("provider %s deploys to %s, outside the EU", [name, region])
}

deny contains msg if {
  some r in input.resource_changes
  r.type == "aws_backup_plan"
  some rule in r.change.after.rule
  some copy in rule.copy_action
  not regex.match("arn:aws:backup:eu-", copy.destination_vault_arn)
  msg := sprintf("backup plan %s copies outside the EU", [r.address])
}
```
nodes.threshold: 0 providers, backup copies or processors outside EU/EEA regions in the infrastructure plan and the processor register

nodes.label: Duplicate delivery harmless
nodes.threshold: Every consumer, given each of its message types twice (and again after a restart), ends in the same state as with one delivery; 0 double effects

nodes.given: a consumer that has handled a message

nodes.when: the same message is delivered again, once right away and once after a restart

nodes.threshold: Every consumer, given each message twice, produces exactly the effects of one delivery

nodes.label: Duplicates handled once
nodes.action: handle a message delivered more than once as once, by recording its id in the same transaction as its effect and keeping the ids for 7 days
nodes.rationale: At-least-once delivery means duplicates; recording the id with the effect is what makes the second delivery harmless even after a crash (microservices.io, Idempotent Consumer).

nodes.label: Duplicates have no effect
nodes.action: acknowledge it without a second effect, recognising it by its message id, which is remembered for at least 72 hours in the same transaction as the effect
nodes.rationale: Brokers and outbox relays deliver at least once, so duplicates are normal; an idempotent consumer makes them harmless (microservices.io, Idempotent consumer).
nodes.unwanted_condition: a consumer receives a message it has already processed

nodes.label: Elevation expires

nodes.when: 4 hours pass

nodes.label: Elevation is approved and expires
nodes.action: grant it only after a second person approves it with a ticket reference, and remove it automatically after at most 4 hours
nodes.rationale: Standing privileges are what attackers look for; time-boxed, approved elevation keeps the window small (NIST SP 800-53 AC-2, AC-6; OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet, least privilege).
nodes.trigger: an operator asks for administrator access to production

nodes.label: Encrypted everywhere

nodes.label: Erasure by key destruction
nodes.action: destroy the person's data key within 24 hours, and its copies in key backups within 35 days, so that their fields in every store, event, log and backup can no longer be decrypted
nodes.rationale: Encrypted data whose key no longer exists cannot be read by anyone, which reaches backups and event streams that cannot be edited (GDPR Art. 17, ICO on erasure of backups).
nodes.trigger: a person's erasure request is accepted, or their data passes its retention period

nodes.label: Erasure on request
nodes.action: erase their data by crypto-shredding in every store, replica, cache, log and export within 30 days, keep only what a legal obligation requires, tell every recipient it was disclosed to, and confirm to the person
nodes.rationale: The right to erasure (GDPR Art. 17) within one month (Art. 12(3)), passed on to the recipients (Art. 19); records the law requires (invoices) are an exception of Art. 17(3)(b).
nodes.trigger: a verified person's erasure request is accepted

nodes.label: Events published with the change
nodes.action: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, publish it to the queue within 5 seconds of the commit, and publish no event whose transaction rolled back
nodes.rationale: A dual write to a database and a broker loses or invents events when either fails; the transactional outbox makes the event part of the commit (microservices.io, Transactional outbox).
nodes.trigger: a transaction changes state that other elements must learn about

nodes.label: Every field classified
nodes.description:
In CI, after the migrations run against an empty database, a query lists the columns without a classification; a new column fails the build until it is classified, and a personal one until the record of processing names it.

Tool: psql in the CI pipeline, against the migrated schema

```sql
-- fails the build when it returns a row
select c.table_name, c.column_name
from information_schema.columns c
join pg_class t on t.relname = c.table_name
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = t.relnamespace and n.nspname = c.table_schema
left join pg_description d on d.objoid = t.oid and d.objsubid = c.ordinal_position
where c.table_schema = 'public'
  and coalesce(d.description, '') !~ '^(personal|not-personal)( |:|$)';
```
nodes.threshold: 0 columns in the migrated schema without a classification (personal or not-personal) in their comment

nodes.label: Every hop mutually authenticated
nodes.action: encrypt the connection with mutual TLS, both sides presenting certificates from the mesh's CA that expire within 24 hours, and refuse a peer without one
nodes.rationale: Encryption and caller identity on every hop, so that a foothold on the network reads nothing and cannot impersonate a service (OWASP TLS Cheat Sheet, client certificates; ASVS 9.2.2).
nodes.trigger: one of our elements connects to another

nodes.label: Every route guarded
nodes.description:
A static rule runs on every pull request and fails on a route registered without going through the authorization module, so a check cannot be forgotten in a handler.

Tool: Semgrep

```yaml
rules:
  - id: route-without-authorize
    languages: [typescript]
    severity: ERROR
    message: Every route goes through authorize(); ADR "Permissions decided in code"
    patterns:
      - pattern: $ROUTER.$METHOD($PATH, ...)
      - metavariable-regex:
          metavariable: $METHOD
          regex: ^(get|post|put|patch|delete)$
      - pattern-not: $ROUTER.$METHOD($PATH, ..., authorize(...), ...)
```
nodes.threshold: 0 routes registered without the authorize middleware

nodes.label: Everyone sees only theirs
nodes.description: People with different jobs, and other systems, use the same element. Each may see and change only what their role, their relation to the record or the policy allows: a check missing at one operation, a check only in the interface, a record fetched by an id the caller should not know, or a list that shows what the detail would refuse each lets data out. Administrators and support need more than everyone else without holding it all the time, and permissions must be taken back when people change jobs or leave.

nodes.label: Failed copies noticed

nodes.label: Failing messages set aside

nodes.rationale: One poisoned message must neither block the rest nor vanish (Enterprise Integration Patterns, Dead Letter Channel).

nodes.label: Just-in-time privileged access
nodes.alternatives:
1. Named standing administrators: simpler, but the rights are there for whoever takes the account.
2. No direct access at all: the strongest, but every support need must be built into the product first.
nodes.consequences:
• A phished operator account gives nothing in production by itself.
• Emergencies need an approver awake, or the break-glass path.
• Every elevation leaves a record of who, why and for how long.
• The elevation tool is itself a critical system to protect.
nodes.context: People and other systems use this element with different rights. The forces: most access-control flaws are not broken sign-ins but a check missing at one operation, or a check on the type of record and not on the record itself (OWASP API1:2023, broken object level authorization); anything the interface hides can still be called; checks scattered through the code drift apart, while a central policy adds a dependency on the request path; administrators and support staff need more than everyone else, and standing privileges are what attackers look for; and permissions accumulate as people change jobs and keep what they had.
nodes.decision: Nobody holds standing administrator rights in production. Operators request elevation with a ticket reference; a second person approves it; it expires after at most 4 hours. Use the platform's mechanism: Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management, AWS IAM Identity Center with temporary elevated access, Google Cloud Privileged Access Manager, or Teleport or HashiCorp Boundary for hosts and databases, chosen by where the infrastructure runs. One sealed break-glass account per environment, its credential split or in a safe, alerts on use and is rotated after it.

nodes.label: Kafka lag and durability
nodes.description:
Prometheus rules over kafka-exporter metrics alert on a consumer group that has messages waiting but has not moved its offset for 5 minutes (the oldest waiting message is at least that old) and on any message published to a .dlq topic.

Tool: Prometheus alerting rules (kafka-exporter)

```yaml
groups:
- name: messaging
  rules:
  - alert: ConsumerStuck
    expr: kafka_consumergroup_lag_sum > 0
      and delta(kafka_consumergroup_current_offset_sum[5m]) == 0
    labels: { severity: page }
    annotations: { summary: "{{ $labels.consumergroup }} has not moved for 5 minutes" }
  - alert: DeadLetters
    expr: increase(kafka_topic_partition_current_offset{topic=~".+\\.dlq"}[5m]) > 0
    labels: { severity: ticket }
```
nodes.threshold: An alert fires when a consumer group with waiting messages has made no progress for 5 minutes, or a dead-letter topic receives a message

nodes.label: Kept in the EU/EEA
nodes.action: store and process personal data only in EU/EEA regions, with backups, logs, support tools and every processor included
nodes.rationale: No transfer outside the EU/EEA, so none of the conditions of GDPR Chapter V (Art. 44-49) has to be met or proven.

nodes.label: Key destroyed
nodes.given: a person whose fields are in the store, an event stream and last night's backup
nodes.then: their key is gone and decrypting any of those copies fails
nodes.when: their erasure is accepted and 24 hours pass

nodes.label: Key material rotated
nodes.action: create new key material automatically, encrypt new data only with it, and keep the older versions for decryption only
nodes.rationale: A cryptoperiod bounds how much data one key protects and how long a leaked key is useful (NIST SP 800-57 Pt 1, 5.3).
nodes.trigger: an encryption key's current material is 365 days old

nodes.label: Key rotation on
nodes.description:
AWS Config reports every customer-managed KMS key whose automatic rotation is off; a scheduled job checks the rotation period of each.

Tool: AWS Config managed rule CMK_BACKING_KEY_ROTATION_ENABLED and the AWS CLI

```bash
for key in $(aws kms list-keys --query 'Keys[].KeyId' --output text); do
  [ "$(aws kms describe-key --key-id "$key" --query 'KeyMetadata.KeyManager' --output text)" = CUSTOMER ] || continue
  status=$(aws kms get-key-rotation-status --key-id "$key" --output json)
  echo "$status" | jq -e --argjson max 365 \
    '.KeyRotationEnabled and (.RotationPeriodInDays <= $max)' >/dev/null \
    || { echo "key $key: rotation off or longer than 365 days"; exit 1; }
done
```
nodes.threshold: 0 customer-managed keys without automatic rotation; rotation period at most 365 days

nodes.label: Key use limited and logged
nodes.action: allow only the element's own identity and the key administrators to use its keys, keep administration and use apart, and log every use of a key for at least 12 months
nodes.rationale: Holding the keys means nothing if anyone can use them; separation of duties and a log of every decryption are what customer-managed keys buy (NIST SP 800-57 Pt 1, 5.3 and 6; OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet, key management).

nodes.label: Mesh in strict mode
nodes.description:
A Conftest policy over the rendered manifests fails when the mesh-wide mutual TLS policy is missing or anything weakens it.

Tool: Conftest (Open Policy Agent) over Istio manifests

```rego
package main

import rego.v1

deny contains msg if {
  input.kind == "PeerAuthentication"
  input.spec.mtls.mode != "STRICT"
  msg := sprintf("%s/%s weakens mutual TLS to %s", [input.metadata.namespace, input.metadata.name, input.spec.mtls.mode])
}

deny contains msg if {
  input.kind == "PeerAuthentication"
  some port, setting in input.spec.portLevelMtls
  setting.mode != "STRICT"
  msg := sprintf("%s/%s turns off mutual TLS on port %v", [input.metadata.namespace, input.metadata.name, port])
}
```
nodes.threshold: A mesh-wide PeerAuthentication in STRICT mode exists, and 0 workloads or namespaces override it to PERMISSIVE or DISABLE

nodes.label: Message schemas in a schema registry
nodes.alternatives:
1. Schemas in the repository with an AsyncAPI diff in CI: no registry to run, but only the producer's repository is checked.
2. Schemaless JSON: nothing to set up, and breaks are found by consumers in production.
nodes.consequences:
• An incompatible schema is refused before any message uses it, across teams.
• Old messages stay readable for as long as they are kept.
• The registry is on the producer's path at start-up and must be highly available.
• Removing a field needs a default first; renaming is add-then-remove.
nodes.context: Parts of the system, or other systems, talk through this queue instead of calling each other. The forces: brokers and networks redeliver, so a message may arrive twice, and avoiding that loses messages instead (exactly once does not exist end to end); a change committed to the database and its message sent to the broker are two writes, and a crash between them keeps one without the other; parallel consumers reorder messages unless order is asked for, and global order does not scale; a message that always fails either blocks the ones behind it or vanishes; producers and consumers are released apart, so a message schema changes while old messages are still waiting; and a backlog grows silently until someone notices that nothing has happened for an hour.
nodes.decision: Every message type has a schema (Avro or Protobuf; JSON Schema where consumers cannot use either) registered in a schema registry under one subject per topic or message type: Confluent Schema Registry or Apicurio Registry with Kafka, AWS Glue Schema Registry on AWS. Subjects are set to BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE, FULL_TRANSITIVE where consumers may be upgraded before producers. Producers fail to start with an unregistered schema (auto.register.schemas = false in production); CI asks the registry whether a changed schema is compatible before merge. The schema version travels in the message.

nodes.label: Message sent with its change
nodes.action: write each message to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the change it reports, and relay it to the broker from there, so that neither the change nor the message exists without the other
nodes.rationale: Writing to the database and then to the broker loses one of the two in a crash between; the outbox makes them one write (microservices.io, Transactional outbox).

nodes.label: Messages arrive and count once
nodes.description: Parts of the system talk through queues. A message can be delivered twice, lost, arrive out of order, or fail every time it is handled; the change it reports can commit while the message is never sent; a producer can change a message so that a consumer released last month cannot read it. Each of these quietly corrupts data, and a stuck consumer looks like silence, unless it is decided how each is handled.

nodes.label: Messages identify themselves
nodes.action: give every message a unique id, its type, its schema version, its source, the time it was produced and a correlation id, as CloudEvents attributes
nodes.rationale: Deduplication, ordering checks, tracing and replay all need these, and a common envelope means every consumer finds them in the same place (CloudEvents specification).

nodes.label: Mutual TLS in a service mesh
nodes.alternatives:
1. TLS on every connection, configured per element: no mesh to run, but no caller identity and more places to get wrong.
2. Clear text inside a private network: simplest, and safe only while the network is ours alone.
nodes.consequences:
• Every hop is encrypted and authenticated without changes to the code.
• Callers inside get identities that authorisation policies can use.
• The mesh is on every request's path: its upgrades and its CA are now critical.
• Traffic to managed services outside the mesh still needs its own TLS settings.
nodes.context: Data reaches this element from people or other systems, or is kept in it. The forces: traffic is read or changed wherever it crosses a network someone else controls, and "inside our network" stops being true with the first misconfigured peering, mirror port or compromised host; old protocol versions and cipher suites stay enabled for years after they are broken; disks, snapshots and backups leave the system in ways nobody tracks; whoever holds the keys can read the data, so who controls them (the provider, us, or only the application) decides who can be compelled or tricked into reading it; certificates and keys that expire or are never rotated cause outages or stay useful to an attacker for years.
nodes.decision: Outside callers get TLS 1.3 only at the edge (Mozilla profile, HSTS); certificates are issued automatically, with ACME or the cloud's certificate manager. Between our own elements, a service mesh in strict mode encrypts and authenticates every hop with mutual TLS and certificates that expire within 24 hours; databases and managed queues outside the mesh are reached with TLS and certificate verification. Choosing the mesh: Linkerd for the least to run and automatic mTLS by default; Istio when you also need fine-grained traffic and authorisation policies; Cilium when it already runs as the network plugin. Judge by the operational load, the sidecar or sidecar-less model and the certificate authority it can chain to.

nodes.label: Newest copy within the RPO
nodes.description:
The backup job pushes the time of its last success (for point-in-time recovery, the exporter reports the last archived log segment); Prometheus pages when the newest copy is older than the RPO, which also catches a job that silently stopped.

Tool: Prometheus (Pushgateway for backup jobs)

```yaml
groups:
  - name: backup-recovery
    rules:
      - alert: RecoveryPointTooOld
        # backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds: pushed by the backup job, or
        # pg_stat_archiver.last_archived_time exported for point-in-time recovery
        expr: time() - backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds{store="orders"} > 0 * 60
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: page }
        annotations:
          summary: 'The newest copy of {{ $labels.store }} is older than 0 minutes'
```
nodes.threshold: The newest recoverable copy is never older than 0 minutes for more than 5 minutes

nodes.label: No overdue grants
nodes.description:
A scheduled CI job runs a query over the grants every day and fails, opening a ticket for the owner, when a grant is overdue for review or belongs to a person who has left.

Tool: psql in a scheduled CI job

```sql
-- fails the job when it returns a row
select g.account_id, g.permission, g.last_reviewed_at, p.left_at
from grants g
join people p on p.account_id = g.account_id
where g.last_reviewed_at < now() - interval '90 days' - interval '14 days'
   or (p.left_at is not null and p.left_at < now() - interval '24 hours');
```
nodes.threshold: 0 grants unreviewed for more than 90 + 14 days; 0 grants of leavers older than 24 hours

nodes.label: No standing admins
nodes.description:
A scheduled query over the cloud account lists the people with administrator policies attached directly; anything returned is a standing right that bypasses elevation. Use the equivalent tables for Azure or Google Cloud.

Tool: Steampipe (AWS plugin)

```sql

select u.name, u.arn
from aws_iam_user u
where u.attached_policy_arns ? 'arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess'
   or u.attached_policy_arns ? 'arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/PowerUserAccess';
```

nodes.label: Older protocols refused
nodes.action: refuse the handshake

nodes.label: One writer per entity

nodes.label: Only the outbox publishes

nodes.label: Only TLS from outside

nodes.rationale: Anything outside crosses networks we do not control; HSTS stops the first request being downgraded (ASVS 9.1.1, 9.1.2; OWASP TLS Cheat Sheet; Mozilla Server Side TLS).

nodes.label: Outbox drained in time
nodes.description:
The database exporter reports the age of the oldest unpublished outbox row; Prometheus pages when the relay falls behind, before consumers notice.

Tool: Prometheus with sql_exporter

```yaml
# sql_exporter collector
collector_name: outbox
metrics:
  - metric_name: outbox_oldest_unpublished_seconds
    type: gauge
    help: 'Age of the oldest event not yet published'
    values: [age]
    query: |
      SELECT coalesce(extract(epoch FROM now() - min(created_at)), 0) AS age FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL
---
# Prometheus alerting rule
groups:
  - name: data-consistency
    rules:
      - alert: OutboxBehind

nodes.label: Permission matrix enforced
nodes.threshold: Every operation called as every role or rule case gives the expected answer, and with another user's record ids returns 403 or 404; 0 mismatches

nodes.label: Permissions by role
nodes.alternatives:
1. Relationships (ReBAC): expresses ownership and sharing, harder to review as a whole.
2. Attribute policies (ABAC): precise, but the attributes have to be kept fresh.
3. Everyone may do everything: only right while nothing is meant for some users.
nodes.consequences:
• One matrix to read, review and test: a test can call every operation as every role.
• Rules that depend on the record (only the owner may edit) do not fit roles and need an explicit check per operation.
• Role explosion when every exception becomes a role.
• Separation of duties can be checked when roles are granted.
nodes.context: People and other systems use this element with different rights. The forces: most access-control flaws are not broken sign-ins but a check missing at one operation, or a check on the type of record and not on the record itself (OWASP API1:2023, broken object level authorization); anything the interface hides can still be called; checks scattered through the code drift apart, while a central policy adds a dependency on the request path; administrators and support staff need more than everyone else, and standing privileges are what attackers look for; and permissions accumulate as people change jobs and keep what they had.
nodes.decision: Users get roles and roles get permissions (NIST core RBAC with static separation of duty), kept in one permission matrix: operation × role, versioned with the code. Every operation checks its permission on the server, on the record it touches as well as its type; anything without a rule is refused. Permissions are decided in the service code; they are taken back through periodic reviews. Keep the roles under about 20: when an exception would become a role, it is a sign that relationships or attributes are needed. Use the framework's role mechanism (Spring Security, ASP.NET Core policies, Pundit, CASL) rather than checks of our own.

nodes.label: Permissions decided in code
nodes.alternatives:
1. A central policy engine (OPA, Cedar, OpenFGA): one place for every service, but a dependency on every request.
2. Checks only at the API gateway: coarse, cannot see the record, and every internal call bypasses them.
nodes.consequences:
• No extra service on the request path; decisions take microseconds.
• Rules change and ship with the code that needs them.
• Each service has its own module: with more services or languages, the rules drift apart.
• Security cannot change a rule without a release of the service.
nodes.context: People and other systems use this element with different rights. The forces: most access-control flaws are not broken sign-ins but a check missing at one operation, or a check on the type of record and not on the record itself (OWASP API1:2023, broken object level authorization); anything the interface hides can still be called; checks scattered through the code drift apart, while a central policy adds a dependency on the request path; administrators and support staff need more than everyone else, and standing privileges are what attackers look for; and permissions accumulate as people change jobs and keep what they had.
nodes.decision: Each service decides permissions in one authorization module, called from one place in the request pipeline (middleware, filter or policy attribute), never from scattered checks in handlers. Use the framework's mechanism: Spring Security method security, ASP.NET Core authorization policies, Pundit or Action Policy (Rails), CASL or Casbin (Node). A static rule fails the build for any route that does not go through the module.

nodes.label: Personal data erased by crypto-shredding
nodes.alternatives:
1. Deletion in every store: no key service, but backups and streams keep the person until they expire.
2. Anonymisation in place: keeps readable history, but must hold against re-identification.
3. One key per store (transparent disk encryption): protects against stolen disks, erases no one.
nodes.consequences:
• One key deletion erases a person everywhere, immutable backups and event streams included.
• Every read of a personal field decrypts: a key cache and the key service's availability are on the hot path.
• Searching, sorting and joining on encrypted fields is not possible; keyed hashes cover exact matches only.
• A lost key store loses everyone's data: the key service needs its own backup and recovery, shorter-lived than 35 days for destroyed keys.
nodes.context: This store keeps data, and some of it may be about people. The forces: data protection law (GDPR) limits why personal data may be processed, for how long it is kept and where it may go, and gives people the rights to get, take away and erase it, each within one month; copies multiply (replicas, backups, logs, exports, analytics, processors) and every one of them has to follow; health, biometric and other special categories carry a higher bar; erasing must not break the records others still need (invoices, the audit trail); and the controller has to be able to prove all of it (accountability, Art. 5(2)).
nodes.decision: Personal data is kept only in the stores and fields the record of processing names, each field classified in the schema. Lawful basis: contract or legal obligation. Location: in the EU/EEA only. Every personal field is encrypted in the application with a data key of its own per person (envelope encryption, AES-256-GCM), the data keys wrapped by a key in a key management service: AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS or Azure Key Vault on that cloud, HashiCorp Vault (Transit) on premises or across clouds; libraries such as AWS Encryption SDK or Google Tink do the envelope work. Erasure destroys the person's data key within 24 hours, which makes their fields in every store, event, log and backup unreadable; key backups expire after 35 days. Unused data is shredded the same way after 60 months. Searchable fields (e-mail for sign-in) are kept as keyed hashes (HMAC) next to the ciphertext.

from presidio_analyzer import AnalyzerEngine

ENTITIES = ["EMAIL_ADDRESS", "PHONE_NUMBER", "IP_ADDRESS", "CREDIT_CARD", "IBAN_CODE", "PERSON"]
analyzer = AnalyzerEngine()
found = 0
with open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for n, line in enumerate(f, 1):

sys.exit(1 if found else 0)
```

nodes.label: Redundant across zones
nodes.alternatives:
1. One zone and fast restarts: cheaper, but one zone outage uses the whole month's budget.
2. Two regions active-active: survives a region, at roughly twice the cost and with the hard problem of data replicated across regions.
nodes.consequences:
• A zone loss costs minutes of errors, not hours.
• Roughly twice the compute of one zone (three zones for 99.95 %), and cross-zone traffic is billed.
• Every instance must be stateless or share state through the database or a cache: sessions and uploads cannot live on one instance.
• The database failover is a few dozen seconds of errors, which counts against the budget; it is tested, not assumed.
nodes.context: People or other systems reach this element, so when it is down somebody notices: a customer who cannot buy, a partner whose calls fail. The forces: every extra nine costs more (more zones, more replicas, automation instead of people) while users cannot tell 99.99 % from 100 % behind their own network; the allowed downtime per 30 days shrinks from hours (99.0 %) to minutes (99.99 %), and a person paged at night needs 15 to 30 minutes just to start; an element is never more available than the product of the hard dependencies it calls; planned work (releases, migrations, patching) is downtime too unless it is designed out; and without an agreed number and a policy for when it is missed, reliability work loses every argument against features.
nodes.decision: The element targets 99.95 % per 30 days. It runs at least two instances in two availability zones (for 99.95 %: three zones, with enough instances that two zones carry the peak), spread with Kubernetes topology spread constraints or zone-redundant platform settings, behind a load balancer that health-checks each instance. Its database fails over to a synchronous standby in another zone by itself: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ, Azure SQL zone-redundant, Cloud SQL high availability or a Patroni cluster. Dependencies: degraded service without them. Planned work: no planned downtime. When the budget is spent: releases freeze. Someone is on call, since 43 minutes (21 for 99.95 %) do not wait for the morning.

nodes.label: Sensitive fields encrypted by the application
nodes.alternatives:
1. Customer-managed keys at rest only: transparent to the application, but visible to anyone who can query.
2. Tokenisation by a vault service (for cards, a PCI provider): takes the data out of scope entirely, adds a dependency.
3. Database column encryption (Always Encrypted, pgcrypto): less code, but keys or plaintext pass through the database.
nodes.consequences:
• Database administrators, backups, replicas and SQL injection see only ciphertext for those fields.
• Those fields cannot be sorted, range-queried or full-text searched in the database.
• Migrations and analytics must go through the application or the KMS to read them.
• Losing the KMS key loses those fields, even in backups.
nodes.context: Data reaches this element from people or other systems, or is kept in it. The forces: traffic is read or changed wherever it crosses a network someone else controls, and "inside our network" stops being true with the first misconfigured peering, mirror port or compromised host; old protocol versions and cipher suites stay enabled for years after they are broken; disks, snapshots and backups leave the system in ways nobody tracks; whoever holds the keys can read the data, so who controls them (the provider, us, or only the application) decides who can be compelled or tricked into reading it; certificates and keys that expire or are never rotated cause outages or stay useful to an attacker for years.
nodes.decision: The application encrypts card numbers, national id numbers, IBANs before writing them, with envelope encryption: AES-256-GCM data keys per record or tenant, wrapped by a customer-managed key in the KMS. Everything else is encrypted at rest under customer-managed keys. Key rotation: automatic rotation of the key material, every 365 days. Library: Google Tink or the AWS Encryption SDK in the element, or HashiCorp Vault Transit when several languages must share the keys; never cryptography written by hand. Fields that must be searched get a separate keyed hash (HMAC-SHA-256) for exact matches.

Tool: GitHub Actions step querying the Prometheus HTTP API

```yaml
- name: Error budget gate
  if: ${{ !contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'reliability-fix') }}
  run: |
    remaining=$(curl -sf "$PROMETHEUS_URL/api/v1/query" \
      --data-urlencode 'query=slo:period_error_budget_remaining:ratio{sloth_service="order-api",sloth_slo="availability"}' \
      | jq -r '.data.result[0].value[1]')
    echo "Error budget remaining: $remaining"
    if awk "BEGIN { exit !($remaining <= 0) }"; then
      echo "::error::Error budget spent: only reliability or security fixes deploy (ADR Spent budget freezes releases)"
      exit 1

nodes.label: Spent budget freezes releases
nodes.alternatives:
1. A review instead of a freeze: keeps shipping, but relies on the review changing priorities.
2. No policy: the target is reported and nothing follows from it.
nodes.consequences:
• Reliability work wins automatically when users are hurting, with no argument.
• A bad month can stop feature releases for days; product owners plan for it.
• The availability measurement must be trusted, since it now gates releases.
• Fixes have to be labelled honestly; the label is reviewed in the pull request.
nodes.context: People or other systems reach this element, so when it is down somebody notices: a customer who cannot buy, a partner whose calls fail. nodes.label: Synchronous replication and backups
nodes.alternatives:
1. Continuous backup with point-in-time recovery: minutes of loss, cheaper and faster writes.
2. Asynchronous replication: fast writes, but what was in flight is lost on failover.
3. Scheduled snapshots: hours of loss.
nodes.consequences:
• No acknowledged write is lost when a zone (or region) is.
• Every write waits for the second copy: higher latency, and writes stop if no synchronous standby is available.
• Twice the database cost, plus the backups that still guard against mistakes.
• Failover must be automatic and tested, or the zero RPO comes with a long RTO.
nodes.context: This store keeps data that the system cannot work without. The forces: stores are lost to broken disks, bad deployments, mistaken deletes, ransomware and region outages, and replication copies the mistakes as faithfully as the data; the less data may be lost (the recovery point objective, RPO) and the faster it must be back (the recovery time objective, RTO), the more every write and every month costs; copies in the same account and region go down, or get encrypted, together with the store; and a backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a copy.
nodes.decision: Writes are replicated synchronously and acknowledged only when a second zone or region has them: PostgreSQL with synchronous_standby_names and synchronous_commit = on (managed by Patroni or CloudNativePG), or a managed service that does it (Amazon Aurora, Azure SQL Business Critical, Cloud SQL high availability; Spanner or CockroachDB across regions). Replication copies mistakes, so continuous backups with point-in-time recovery cover them, kept 35 days in another account and region, locked. Region loss: a warm standby in a second region. Service comes back within 30 minutes. Proven by an automated restore test every week. Choose a managed service unless the database must run on premises; choose cross-region synchronous replication only when the added latency of every write (tens of milliseconds) is acceptable.

metrics:

    help: 'Standbys replicating synchronously'
    values: [n]
    query: |
      SELECT count(*) AS n FROM pg_stat_replication WHERE sync_state IN ('sync', 'quorum')
---
# Prometheus alerting rule
groups:
  - name: backup-recovery
    rules:
      - alert: NoSynchronousStandby
        expr: pg_sync_standbys < 1
        for: 1m
        labels: { severity: page }
```

nodes.label: Transactional outbox
nodes.alternatives:
1. Publish after commit (dual write): simpler, but a crash between commit and publish loses the event.
2. Event sourcing: the events are the state, which removes the dual write but changes the whole persistence model.
3. Two-phase commit between database and broker: blocking and seldom supported.
nodes.consequences:
• No lost or invented events: an event exists if and only if its change committed.
• Delivery is at least once, so every consumer must be idempotent.
• Others see the change up to 5 seconds later; the relay's lag must be watched.
• The outbox table needs cleaning up, and event order holds only per aggregate key.
nodes.context: This element writes to stores and queues, and one business operation often changes several records, sometimes in several stores or services. The forces: a crash between two writes leaves half an operation behind; writing to a database and then to a broker (a dual write) loses or invents events when either fails; concurrent transactions at the default isolation level lose updates and break invariants that span rows; brokers deliver at least once, so every message may come twice; replicas and caches lag, so a user may not see what they just saved; and when several elements write the same data, nobody knows which copy is the truth.
nodes.decision: State changes and the events that announce them are written in one local transaction: the event goes to an outbox table, and a relay publishes it to the broker within 5 seconds, then marks it sent. The relay is change data capture with Debezium (its outbox event router) when Kafka Connect is already run, otherwise a polling publisher, or the framework's outbox (Spring Modulith event publication registry, MassTransit or NServiceBus outbox). Nothing publishes to the broker directly. Consumers are idempotent: they remember message ids for 72 hours in the same transaction as their effect. Isolation: Serializable. Reads: replicas, with read-your-writes. Writers: one owning element per entity.

nodes.label: Users sign in through an identity provider
nodes.alternatives:
1. Our own user store: full control of the experience, but you own password storage, lockout, MFA and breach response.
2. Server-side sessions only (cookies): simple for one web app, awkward for APIs called by other systems and mobile clients.
3. Long-lived tokens without revocation: fewer calls to the provider, but a stolen token works until it expires.
nodes.consequences:
• No passwords to store, reset or leak; MFA, lockout and breached-password checks come from the provider.
• The provider is on the sign-in path: when it is down nobody new signs in, sessions already open keep working until they expire.
• Revocation within 60 s means short-lived access tokens and a refresh on every expiry, a little more traffic to the provider.
• Who may do what (authorisation) is still yours to design: a valid token says who, not what.
nodes.context: People or other systems reach this element from outside, so it must know who is calling before it acts for them. The forces: credentials leak and get guessed (credential stuffing tries billions of leaked pairs); sessions outlive the person on a shared or lost device; self-contained tokens stay valid until they expire unless revocation is designed in; other systems call too, and a call from inside the network is not a call from a known system; and after an incident the record of who did what has to hold.
nodes.decision: Users sign in through an external identity provider with OpenID Connect (authorization code flow with PKCE); we store no password. Sessions end after 15 minutes without a request and are revoked within 60 seconds: access tokens live no longer than that, and refresh tokens are rotated on use and checked against a revocation list. Calls from other systems: OAuth 2.0 client credentials. Operations open without sign-in are on a public list kept in the code. Choosing the provider: the one the users' organisation already runs (Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace) for business users; Auth0, Cognito or Keycloak for consumers, by cost per active user and where the data may be kept.

nodes.label: Weekly restore test
nodes.description:

Tool: GitHub Actions (scheduled workflow)

```yaml
# .github/workflows/restore-drill.yml
name: restore-drill
on:
  schedule: [{ cron: '0 3 * * 1' }]   # every Monday, 03:00 UTC
  workflow_dispatch: {}
jobs:
  restore:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Restore the latest copy into a clean environment
        run: ./ops/recover.sh --target "drill-$GITHUB_RUN_ID" --latest
      - name: Check row counts, newest timestamp and a sample of records
        run: ./ops/verify.sh --target "drill-$GITHUB_RUN_ID" --max-age-minutes 0
      - name: Tear down
        if: always()
        run: ./ops/teardown.sh "drill-$GITHUB_RUN_ID"
```

need-corporate-feedback.description:
Notes from the quarterly call with the treasurer of one of our larger corporate clients:

- Payroll goes in as one bulk file of about 4,000 lines. Last month one bad IBAN stopped the file halfway and half the staff were paid a day late. They want to hear about all problems before anything is sent.
- Their auditors require a second signatory on every batch; today they enforce it by e-mail.
- They would like to see afterwards who approved what.
need-corporate-feedback.label: Corporate treasurer feedback
need-corporate-feedback.source: Relationship manager — quarterly call with a corporate client

need-regulation.description:
Summary of the regulatory obligations attached to our EU payment-institution licence:

- PSD2: every payment initiated from a digital channel needs strong customer authentication, and customers must see all charges and the exchange rate before they confirm.
- AMLD6: no account may be used before customer due diligence (identity, sanctions, PEP and AML screening) is complete.
- Record keeping: decisions on suspicious payments must be reconstructable for at least five years, including who decided and why.
need-regulation.label: PSD2 & AMLD6 obligations

need-retail-brief.description:
Our customers move money from the mobile app and the web, and they need to trust what they see.

Support tells us people send a payment again when they are not sure the first one went through; duplicates are the top reason for calls. Balances in the app sometimes disagree with statements for a few minutes, and that worries people. Last quarter we refunded €1.2M of authorised push-payment fraud, and most of it could have been stopped if someone had looked at the payment before it left.

We want customers to always know where a payment is, to see the same balance everywhere, and suspicious payments to be caught before settlement.
need-retail-brief.label: Retail payments brief
need-retail-brief.source: Head of Digital Payments — product kick-off

req-balance-ledger.action: derive every displayed balance and statement from the immutable transaction ledger
req-balance-ledger.label: Balances from the ledger
req-balance-ledger.rationale: One source of truth: what the customer sees is what the auditor sees.

req-bulk-validation.action: validate every line (IBAN checksum, amount, duplicate reference) and report all errors before any payment in the batch is released
req-bulk-validation.label: Validate bulk files up front
req-bulk-validation.rationale: Partially executed payroll batches are expensive to unwind.
req-bulk-validation.trigger: a corporate client uploads a bulk payment file

req-case-audit.action: record every operator decision on a fraud case, with reason and timestamp, in an append-only audit trail
req-case-audit.label: Auditable case decisions
req-case-audit.rationale: Regulators ask why a payment was released; the answer has to be reconstructable years later.

req-dual-approval.action: require approval by a second authorised signatory before the batch is submitted
req-dual-approval.label: Four-eyes approval
req-dual-approval.precondition: a bulk batch totals more than €100,000
req-dual-approval.rationale: Corporate mandate rules; also an internal-fraud control.

req-fraud-hold.action: hold the payment, tell the customer it is under review and open a fraud case for an operator
req-fraud-hold.label: Hold high-risk payments
req-fraud-hold.rationale: Authorised push-payment fraud is refundable to the customer — stopping it before settlement is far cheaper.
req-fraud-hold.unwanted_condition: the fraud score of a payment exceeds the risk threshold

req-fx-transparency.action: show the exchange rate, all fees and the amount the recipient receives before the customer confirms
req-fx-transparency.feature: a payment is cross-border or in a foreign currency
req-fx-transparency.label: FX & fee transparency
req-fx-transparency.rationale: PSD2 / Cross-Border Payments Regulation — no hidden mark-ups.

req-kyc.action: verify identity and screen against sanctions and AML lists before any account is activated
req-kyc.label: KYC before activation
req-kyc.rationale: AMLD6 — no account may be used before due diligence is complete.

req-payment-status.action: show a confirmation with the payment reference and expected settlement date within 2 seconds
req-payment-status.label: Instant payment confirmation
req-payment-status.rationale: Customers retry payments they are unsure about; duplicate payments are the #1 support topic.
req-payment-status.trigger: a payment is accepted for execution

req-psd2.action: comply with PSD2 for every payment initiated through a digital channel
req-psd2.label: PSD2-compliant payments
req-psd2.rationale: Operating licence condition in the EU; the child requirements break it down into testable behaviour.

req-sca.action: require strong customer authentication with two independent factors before the payment is released
req-sca.label: Strong customer authentication
req-sca.rationale: PSD2 RTS on SCA. Approving in the bound mobile app covers possession + inherence.
req-sca.trigger: a customer submits a payment above €30
